questions.t: An engineer rereads her handover note, judges it perfectly clear and sends it; the new hire replies asking what "the Q-pipeline" is and where to start. Her self-check failed because of the curse of knowledge.
questions.f: An engineer rereads her handover note, judges it perfectly clear and sends it; the new hire replies asking what "the Q-pipeline" is and where to start. Her self-check failed because of information overload.
questions.x: The tell is internal shorthand plus a clarity check done by rereading it herself, the very judgment the curse of knowledge distorts. The note isn't too long; it is missing background she can no longer imagine lacking.

questions.t: To catch the curse of knowledge in a draft, ask a few people from the target audience to explain a section in their own words, and revise wherever they misread it.
questions.f: To catch the curse of knowledge in a draft, ask a few people from the target audience "Is this clear?", and revise wherever they say no.
questions.x: Readers can say a text is clear and still misread it, so a yes/no question gives you no real signal. A paraphrase test, recorded without correcting them, shows exactly where your missing context trips them up.

questions.t: In seven large-sample experiments, Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt estimated the adult false-belief curse-of-knowledge effect at less than half its originally reported size.
questions.f: In seven large-sample experiments, Ryskin and Brown-Schmidt estimated the adult false-belief curse-of-knowledge effect at more than twice its originally reported size.
questions.x: Their high-powered re-estimate shrank the effect, which is why the evidence is rated mixed: the direction is consistent, but early estimates were inflated and real-world size is uncertain.

questions.t: A manager tells a colleague from a blunter culture that a report is "perhaps not quite there yet", and the colleague sends it unchanged. The manager's phrase was a downgrader, softening a serious problem into what sounded like a suggestion.
questions.f: A manager tells a colleague from a blunter culture that a report is "perhaps not quite there yet", and the colleague sends it unchanged. The manager's phrase was an upgrader, sharpening the criticism so it sounded harsher than meant.
questions.x: Words like "perhaps" and understatement such as "not quite there" are downgraders that cushion criticism. Decoded in a direct style, the warning was heard as optional; upgraders are intensifiers like "totally" or "absolutely".

questions.t: After giving criticism across a directness gap, ask the person what they will do differently; an answer smaller or bigger than the problem shows your message was decoded in the other style.
questions.f: After giving criticism across a directness gap, ask the person whether you came across as polite; a yes shows your message was decoded the way you meant it.
questions.x: Politeness tells you how the delivery felt, not what was understood. Asking about their next step tests whether the size of the problem landed, which is where style mismatches go wrong.

questions.t: Sanchez-Burks and colleagues found Americans became less indirect at work than in social settings, while East Asian participants did not shift that way.
questions.f: Sanchez-Burks and colleagues found East Asian participants became less indirect at work than in social settings, while Americans did not shift that way.
questions.x: The work-versus-social drop in indirectness appeared for Americans, not for Korean and Chinese participants, suggesting a cultural schema switched on by the workplace rather than a fixed national trait.

questions.t: Upset about a missed deadline, a project lead tells a colleague, "I feel that you don't respect my time." That is a disguised accusation, not a real I-statement.
questions.f: Upset about a missed deadline, a project lead tells a colleague, "I feel that you don't respect my time." That is a well-formed I-statement, because it opens with "I feel".
questions.x: "I feel that you..." puts a verdict about the other person's motives behind an I. A real I-statement names an observable behaviour, its concrete effect and an actual emotion such as worry or frustration.

questions.t: After delivering an I-statement, stop and listen, reflect back the other person's reaction, and send a clearer second I-statement only if the first was misunderstood.
questions.f: After delivering an I-statement, repeat it more firmly each time the other person pushes back, until they agree to change the behaviour.
questions.x: Some defensiveness is expected, and Gordon paired I-messages with active listening so the speaker shifts to listening once the other person reacts. Restating louder turns the exchange back into a contest.

questions.t: Korobov's analysis of couples' everyday arguments found I-language on its own rarely de-escalated them; showing awareness of the partner's feelings helped more.
questions.f: Korobov's analysis of couples' everyday arguments found I-language on its own reliably de-escalated them, whatever else the speaker said.
questions.x: In naturally occurring arguments the pronoun alone did little; what helped was visible awareness of the other person's feelings or the relationship. That's why the technique's evidence is rated mixed.

questions.t: A team lead starts a long email thread to get four managers to agree how to split a disputed budget. Media synchronicity theory would call this a convergence job, better served by a live discussion.
questions.f: A team lead starts a long email thread to get four managers to agree how to split a disputed budget. Media synchronicity theory would call this a conveyance job, well served by email.
questions.x: Reaching agreement on a contested question is convergence, which fast-feedback live channels support. Conveyance is passing on information people can absorb alone, such as updates or data, where email works well.

questions.t: After settling a contested decision on a call, send a same-day written recap of the decision, owners and dates.
questions.f: After settling a contested decision on a call, book a second call to confirm the decision, owners and dates instead of writing them down.
questions.x: Live talk is good for reaching agreement but leaves nothing to reread. Mixing channels (facts in writing, discussion live, recap in writing) locks in the shared understanding; another call still leaves no record.

questions.t: In experiments reported in 2005, email readers identified whether statements were sarcastic or serious only about 56% of the time, though senders expected about 78%.
questions.f: In experiments reported in 2005, email readers identified whether statements were sarcastic or serious about 78% of the time, slightly beating the 56% senders expected.
questions.x: Kruger, Epley and colleagues found email readers barely beat chance while senders were confident their tone would land; voice listeners did much better. Text strips out tone, and senders rarely notice.

questions.t: A risk update reads: "We judge it very likely (80-95%) the launch slips, and we have moderate confidence in that." Under ICD 203 practice, that sentence should be split, because it mixes likelihood and confidence.
questions.f: A risk update reads: "We judge it very likely (80-95%) the launch slips, and we have moderate confidence in that." Under ICD 203 practice, that sentence is ideal, because it pairs likelihood and confidence.
questions.x: Likelihood is how probable the event is; confidence is how solid the evidence is. ICD 203 requires that confidence never share a sentence with a likelihood term, so readers don't blur the two.

questions.t: When you use a likelihood word in a client update, put its numeric range in brackets right after it, as in "likely (55-80%)", rather than in a key at the end.
questions.f: When you use a likelihood word in a client update, put the numeric ranges in a key at the end, rather than in brackets right after the word.
questions.x: In the 2019 Wintle experiment, in-text brackets were the only format that substantially improved agreement; linked tables and tooltips helped little, partly because only about half of readers looked at them.

questions.t: CIA estimator Sherman Kent argued in a 1964 essay that likelihood words need agreed numeric meanings, after colleagues read "serious possibility" as anything from unlikely to likely.
questions.f: CIA estimator Sherman Kent argued in a 1951 essay that likelihood words need agreed numeric meanings, after colleagues read "serious possibility" as anything from unlikely to likely.
questions.x: The 1964 Studies in Intelligence essay looked back at a 1951 estimate that called an attack a "serious possibility"; 1951 is when the vague estimate was written, not when Kent proposed the fix.

questions.t: A lead tells an analyst, "When Priya asked where the churn figure came from, you said 'I'd have to check' and moved on." In SBI, that line is the behaviour step.
questions.f: A lead tells an analyst, "When Priya asked where the churn figure came from, you said 'I'd have to check' and moved on." In SBI, that line is the impact step.
questions.x: It describes what a camera could have recorded: words said and an action taken. The impact step would name the consequence, such as lost agenda time or VPs doubting the forecast, and the lead's reaction.

questions.t: When SBI feedback is meant to change a behaviour, ask what the person was aiming for and listen before suggesting any fix.
questions.f: When SBI feedback is meant to change a behaviour, give your fix straight after the impact and ask about intent only if they push back.
questions.x: The intent question turns feedback into a two-way coaching conversation and guards against treating a bad impact as a bad motive. Leading with the fix skips the listening the technique depends on.

questions.t: Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found that feedback improved performance on average, yet more than a third of feedback interventions made performance worse.
questions.f: Kluger and DeNisi's 1996 meta-analysis found that feedback improved performance on average, and fewer than one in twenty feedback interventions made performance worse.
questions.x: Over a third of interventions backfired, which the authors linked to feedback pulling attention from the task toward the self. SBI's task-focused, specific structure is meant to stay on the helpful side.

questions.t: An analyst emails a VP who must approve a forecast, copying finance, and opens with the formula changes in tab 3. The email was written for the secondary technical readers, not the primary reader who must act.
questions.f: An analyst emails a VP who must approve a forecast, copying finance, and opens with the formula changes in tab 3. The email was written for the primary reader who must act, as audience analysis advises.
questions.x: Audience analysis starts with the person who must decide and leads with what matters to them, here the approval and its impact. Formula detail belongs in a separate section for the technical readers.

questions.t: When one document must serve both executives and technical reviewers, give each group its own clearly labelled section.
questions.f: When one document must serve both executives and technical reviewers, blend both groups' material into every paragraph so neither feels left out.
questions.x: Mixing material for different readers confuses everyone. Separate, labelled sections let the primary reader get what they need up front while technical readers find the detail they want.

questions.t: In Lane and Ferreira's 2008 experiments, drawing speakers' attention to information their partner couldn't see made them mention it to the partner more often.
questions.f: In Lane and Ferreira's 2008 experiments, drawing speakers' attention to information their partner couldn't see made them mention it to the partner less often.
questions.x: Salient private information leaked into descriptions more, and partners then erred on about a third of them. Adapting to an audience is fragile under load, which is why a written profile and a real-reader check help.

questions.t: In a planning meeting a manager asks, "Don't you think we should launch Monday?" That is a leading question that signals the answer she wants.
questions.f: In a planning meeting a manager asks, "Don't you think we should launch Monday?" That is an open-ended question that lets the team explain in their own words.
questions.x: It can be settled with yes or no and builds the manager's preferred answer into the question. An open version would be something like "What would need to be true for a Monday launch?"

questions.t: When you need a firm answer on a known risk, such as whether a release will slip past the 30th, ask a direct, specific question rather than an open one.
questions.f: When you need a firm answer on a known risk, such as whether a release will slip past the 30th, ask a broad open question like "How's it going?"
questions.x: Open questions are for exploring; commitments and specific facts call for closed, pointed questions. Very general questions invite "fine" and leave room to dodge.

questions.t: Minson and colleagues found that questions presuming a problem exists, such as "What problems have you had with it?", drew more honest disclosure of bad news than general ones.
questions.f: Minson and colleagues found that general questions, such as "What do you think of it?", drew more honest disclosure of bad news than ones presuming a problem exists.
questions.x: In written tasks and face-to-face meetings, problem-presuming questions surfaced concealed issues best, and general questions did worst. It challenges the idea that a neutral open question is always most revealing.

questions.t: A project lead opens a status meeting with "We're on track, right?", gets nods, and hears about an integration slip afterwards in the corridor. That points to low psychological safety in the meeting.
questions.f: A project lead opens a status meeting with "We're on track, right?", gets nods, and hears about an integration slip afterwards in the corridor. That points to high psychological safety, since no one disagreed.
questions.x: Real discussion happening in the hallway rather than the room is a classic low-safety sign: people judged that raising bad news in front of the group was risky. Silence in the meeting isn't agreement.

questions.t: To make it safer to raise problems in a status meeting, a leader can go first by naming something she got wrong or doesn't know.
questions.f: To make it safer to raise problems in a status meeting, a leader should first present the plan as settled, so the team sees confidence before voicing doubts.
questions.x: Modelling fallibility lowers the price of the next admission, and framing the work as a learning problem invites every view. Presenting the plan as settled tells people the answer is already decided.

questions.t: Psychological safety means people can admit mistakes and challenge each other without being punished; it doesn't mean being comfortable or free of accountability.
questions.f: Psychological safety means keeping meetings comfortable and shielding people from accountability for poor work.
questions.x: It is about candour, and productive disagreement can feel uncomfortable even in a safe team. Leaders can still decline proposals and address poor work while keeping it safe to speak up.

questions.t: Opening a contract renewal, an operations manager tells the vendor, "We really can't move away from you, so do what you can on price." He has revealed a weak BATNA, which negotiation guidance says to keep private.
questions.f: Opening a contract renewal, an operations manager tells the vendor, "We really can't move away from you, so do what you can on price." He has revealed a strong BATNA, which negotiation guidance says to mention early.
questions.x: Saying you can't leave tells the vendor your alternative to a deal is poor, handing them leverage. Guidance is to keep a weak BATNA to yourself and, if strong, mention it later rather than as an opening threat.

questions.t: Before treating a competing quote as your BATNA, translate it into the same terms as the deal on the table: total cost, coverage, timing and switching effort.
questions.f: Before treating a competing quote as your BATNA, compare its headline price with the deal on the table; coverage, timing and switching effort can be sorted out later.
questions.x: An alternative judged on its headline number can look better than it is, as in the homeowner whose 30%-cheaper policy turned out worse on limits and exclusions. Only a like-for-like comparison tells you which option truly wins.

questions.t: Schaerer, Swaab and Galinsky found that sellers with a weak alternative felt more powerful than sellers with none, yet made lower first offers and reached less profitable deals.
questions.f: Schaerer, Swaab and Galinsky found that sellers with a weak alternative felt more powerful than sellers with none, and made higher first offers and reached more profitable deals.
questions.x: The weak alternative acted as a low anchor on the opening ask. That's why a weak BATNA should set your walk-away point, while your first offer is anchored on your goal.

questions.t: A presentation coach tells a team their slide content barely matters because 93% of communication is nonverbal. That stretches Mehrabian's studies, which measured judgments of liking from conflicting cues in single-word tasks.
questions.f: A presentation coach tells a team their slide content barely matters because 93% of communication is nonverbal. That follows Mehrabian's studies, which measured how much meaning words carry in work briefings.
questions.x: The 7-38-55 split came from two narrow 1967 lab studies of liking, with the verbal channel nearly empty by design. Mehrabian says it doesn't apply to communication in general; in briefings, words carry most of the information.

questions.t: When praising a colleague, put your phone away and let your tone match your words, because when cues about feelings conflict, listeners tend to trust the tone and face.
questions.f: When praising a colleague, the exact words matter more than tone or attention, because when cues about feelings conflict, listeners tend to trust the words.
questions.x: The part of Mehrabian's finding that survives is narrow: with mixed emotional signals, people believe the nonverbal cue. Flat praise while checking a phone reads as insincere, however well worded.

questions.t: In Zuckerman and colleagues' 1982 honesty-judging study, once full speech was present, adding verbal content improved judges' accuracy far more than adding the face did.
questions.f: In Zuckerman and colleagues' 1982 honesty-judging study, once full speech was present, adding the face improved judges' accuracy far more than adding verbal content did.
questions.x: The face looked dominant in earlier work only when speech was filtered out or cut to one word. With real speech, words mattered, and no single channel always won.

questions.t: A program manager needs time from a security reviewer she can't direct, and offers to present the reviewer's findings by name at the quarterly leadership review. In Cohen and Bradford's model, that is a position-related currency.
questions.f: A program manager needs time from a security reviewer she can't direct, and offers to present the reviewer's findings by name at the quarterly leadership review. In Cohen and Bradford's model, that is a task-related currency.
questions.x: Recognition and visibility with leadership are position-related currencies. Task-related ones are resources, assistance, information or fast response, which this offer doesn't provide.

questions.t: When a peer in another team keeps declining to help, find out how they're measured and what pressures they face this quarter before asking again.
questions.f: When a peer in another team keeps declining to help, escalate early to your shared boss, since a manager's request carries more weight than yours.
questions.x: The model starts by treating the person as a potential ally and diagnosing their world. Escalating is a negative currency that can spiral into mutual retaliation and damages the relationship you'll need again.

questions.t: Yukl and Tracey's 1992 study found exchange and ingratiation helped moderately when influencing peers and subordinates, but not when influencing bosses.
questions.f: Yukl and Tracey's 1992 study found exchange and ingratiation helped most when influencing bosses, but not when influencing peers and subordinates.
questions.x: Rational persuasion, inspirational appeals and consultation won commitment in every direction; trade-based tactics only helped sideways and downward. Overt quid-pro-quo is the weakest part of the influence model's evidence.

questions.t: Hands shaking before her first leadership briefing, an analyst tells herself, "My heart's racing because this matters; I'm excited to get the forecast approved." That is anxiety reappraisal.
questions.f: Hands shaking before her first leadership briefing, an analyst tells herself, "My heart's racing because this matters; I'm excited to get the forecast approved." That is a relaxation technique for lowering her arousal.
questions.x: She accepts the arousal and relabels it as excitement aimed at an opportunity, rather than trying to calm down. Reappraisal changes what the jitters mean; it doesn't try to switch them off.

questions.t: Use anxiety reappraisal in the final minutes before a talk as an add-on to rehearsal, not as a substitute for knowing your material.
questions.f: Use anxiety reappraisal in place of rehearsal when time is short, since relabelling nerves as excitement makes up for thin preparation.
questions.x: No study tested reappraisal instead of preparation; it changes how the nerves feel, not whether you know the content. Rehearse first, then use the reframe just before you start.

questions.t: A 2025 direct replication of Brooks's public-speaking study found that saying "I am excited" made people feel more excited, but observers rated their speeches no better.
questions.f: A 2025 direct replication of Brooks's public-speaking study found that saying "I am excited" left people feeling no more excited, yet observers rated their speeches better.
questions.x: The replication kept the feeling shift but lost the performance gain on every observer rating, which is why the technique's evidence is contested. It is cheap to try, but don't count on it to impress the audience.

questions.t: Before going on leave, a lead hands over a client escalation and asks, "If the patch fails Thursday, what are your next two moves, and who hears from you first?" That is teach-back.
questions.f: Before going on leave, a lead hands over a client escalation and asks, "If the patch fails Thursday, what are your next two moves, and who hears from you first?" That is paraphrasing.
questions.x: The explainer is asking the listener to restate the plan in their own words to check the explanation landed. Paraphrasing is the mirror image: the listener restates on their own initiative.

questions.t: When asking for a teach-back, frame it as a check on your own explanation, as in "I want to make sure I explained that clearly."
questions.f: When asking for a teach-back, frame it as a check on their attention, as in "Let's see whether you were listening."
questions.x: Owning the check keeps the other person's dignity intact and makes it easy to admit a gap. A check that sounds like an exam feels patronising and invites a defensive "yes, got it".

questions.t: In Schillinger and colleagues' 2003 study of diabetes visits, physicians checked patients' recall or comprehension in only 20% of visits.
questions.f: In Schillinger and colleagues' 2003 study of diabetes visits, physicians checked patients' recall or comprehension in about 80% of visits.
questions.x: Checking was rare: 20% of visits and 12% of new concepts. Where it happened, patients had better blood-sugar control, and visits weren't longer. The study was small and observational, so it shows association, not cause.

questions.t: A team lead asking a steering committee to fund a test environment frames her case around future benefits and risks. In Aristotle's terms, that fits an audience judging what is advantageous for the future.
questions.f: A team lead asking a steering committee to fund a test environment frames her case around who caused past outages. In Aristotle's terms, that fits an audience judging what is advantageous for the future.
questions.x: Aristotle defines each kind of speech by what its audience must judge: an assembly decides future advantage, a court judges past acts. A funding decision is forward-looking, so blame for past failures is the wrong frame.

questions.t: Aristotle defines rhetoric as the capacity to see the available means of persuasion in a given case, not as actually winning the audience over.
questions.f: Aristotle defines rhetoric as actually winning the audience over, so a speaker who fails to persuade has not mastered the art.
questions.x: Like a doctor who does everything possible without curing every patient, a speaker has mastered rhetoric by seeing every available means, even if a stubborn audience isn't persuaded.

questions.t: Aristotle's Rhetoric answers Plato, whose Gorgias had dismissed rhetoric as a knack without knowledge.
questions.f: Aristotle's Rhetoric answers Cicero, whose writings had dismissed rhetoric as a knack without knowledge.
questions.x: Plato's Gorgias set the challenge, and Aristotle replied by calling rhetoric a counterpart of dialectic. Cicero came centuries later and borrowed from the Rhetoric rather than prompting it.

questions.t: A release note reads, "The team shipped the fix last night." An editor flags it as passive because it describes the past, but the sentence is already in active voice.
questions.f: A release note reads, "The team shipped the fix last night." An editor flags it as passive because it describes the past, and the sentence should be rewritten into active voice.
questions.x: The doer, the team, is the subject, so the sentence is active; past tense is a separate question from voice. A passive would look like "The fix was shipped", a form of "to be" plus a past participle.

questions.t: To fix "Open issues must be resolved before the release is approved" in a client email, name who acts: "Your team needs to fix open issues by Thursday, then I'll approve the release."
questions.f: To fix "Open issues must be resolved before the release is approved" in a client email, just add a date: "Open issues must be resolved by Thursday before approval."
questions.x: The original's real flaw is that no one owns the work, so each side can assume the other will do it. A deadline alone keeps that gap; putting the actor first assigns each task.

questions.t: In Paolazzi and colleagues' 2019 experiments, passives were read faster than matched active sentences, but readers answered who-did-what questions less accurately after them.
questions.f: In Paolazzi and colleagues' 2019 experiments, passives were read more slowly than matched active sentences, but readers answered who-did-what questions just as accurately after them.
questions.x: Speed favoured passives, yet accuracy about who did what dropped, a difficulty the authors place in remembering the sentence, not parsing it. That supports naming the actor when responsibility matters.

questions.t: A manager leaves a project review sure her disappointment over the slipped milestone was plain on her face, then is surprised when the lead calls the review "positive." She was caught by the illusion of transparency.
questions.f: A manager leaves a project review sure her disappointment over the slipped milestone was plain on her face, then is surprised when the lead calls the review "positive." She was caught by the curse of knowledge.
questions.x: She overestimated how visible her own feeling was, which is the illusion of transparency. The curse of knowledge is about overestimating what others know; the fix here is to say the concern in words.

questions.t: When a chat message depends on tone, such as a deadpan joke or mild annoyance, state the intent in words ("this is a joke", "I'm concerned about this date") rather than trusting tone to carry it.
questions.f: When a chat message depends on tone, such as a deadpan joke or mild annoyance, keep it short and trust a colleague who knows you well to read the tone correctly.
questions.x: Email senders overestimate how well sarcasm, anger or humour come through, even with people who know them. Naming the intent removes the guesswork that text can't carry.

questions.t: In Keysar and Henly's 2002 study, when speakers believed a listener had understood an ambiguous sentence, the listener had in fact misunderstood it 46% of the time.
questions.f: In Keysar and Henly's 2002 study, when speakers believed a listener had understood an ambiguous sentence, the listener had in fact misunderstood it 6% of the time.
questions.x: Nearly half of the cases speakers counted as understood were misunderstandings, which is why the advice is to expect miscommunication and check. A 6% miss rate would make the bias trivial.

questions.t: Before a first call with a new supplier team in Japan, a manager plans to leave the key terms implied, reasoning that Japan is a high-context culture. That leans on country rankings the research has largely failed to support.
questions.f: Before a first call with a new supplier team in Japan, a manager plans to leave the key terms implied, reasoning that Japan is a high-context culture. That is a well-supported use of Hall's model.
questions.x: The tell is inferring someone's style from a passport. Reviews found the country placements weakly supported, so ask how much context this team shares and default to explicit terms.

questions.t: In a newly formed team whose members share little background, state each decision, owner and deadline explicitly, and confirm in writing what was agreed after the meeting.
questions.f: In a newly formed team whose members share little background, leave decisions loosely stated at first and let a shared understanding build over the next few meetings.
questions.x: When context isn't shared, nothing fills the gaps that implicit messages leave, so explicit, written confirmation is the safe default. Waiting for understanding to build risks people leaving with different versions of the decision.

questions.t: Cardon's review of contexting studies found communication channel was the best-supported part of the high/low-context model, while most studies of directness did not support it.
questions.f: Cardon's review of contexting studies found directness was the best-supported part of the high/low-context model, while most studies of communication channel did not support it.
questions.x: Directness is the part most often discussed, yet it fared worst in the empirical tests; channel preferences held up best. That is one reason the model is treated as contested.

questions.t: A designer emails a director with the subject "Quick question" and three paragraphs of project history before finally asking for sign-off on the mockups by Friday. The email buries its request.
questions.f: A designer emails a director with the subject "Quick question" and three paragraphs of project history before finally asking for sign-off on the mockups by Friday. The email is well built, giving context before the ask.
questions.x: A vague subject and an ask hidden under background are two classic email pitfalls. A better version names the action in the subject and opens with the sign-off request and its Friday deadline.

questions.t: When you send a non-urgent work email late in the evening, add a line saying the reply can wait until working hours.
questions.f: When you send a non-urgent work email late in the evening, send it without comment, since the reader can tell from the timestamp that it isn't urgent.
questions.x: Receivers of off-hours email tend to assume senders want faster replies than they do. A one-line note about timing closed that gap in the urgency-bias studies; silence leaves the reader guessing.

questions.t: In Kushlev and Dunn's 2015 field experiment, people told to check email three times a day with notifications off reported lower daily stress than in a week of unlimited checking.
questions.f: In Kushlev and Dunn's 2015 field experiment, people told to check email three times a day with notifications off reported higher daily stress than in a week of unlimited checking.
questions.x: Batching email checks lowered daily stress in this exploratory study, though it did not change overall weekly stress. The finding supports checking on purpose rather than reacting to every notification.

questions.t: In a one-on-one a tester says the sprint scope keeps changing. Her lead replies, "So the mid-sprint changes leave you rushed and worried about quality, but the client already agreed, so we can't move it." The restatement was a lead-in to rebuttal.
questions.f: In a one-on-one a tester says the sprint scope keeps changing. Her lead replies, "So the mid-sprint changes leave you rushed and worried about quality, but the client already agreed, so we can't move it." That is paraphrasing done well.
questions.x: The "but" straight after the restatement, with no check question, gives it away: the paraphrase set up an argument. Done well, it ends with "Have I got that right?" and holds the lead's own view until she confirms.

questions.t: When an operations lead says a vendor's Tuesday deliveries clash with the weekly stock count, restate the clash and the worry behind it in your own words and ask whether that is the main problem, before defending the schedule.
questions.f: When an operations lead says a vendor's Tuesday deliveries clash with the weekly stock count, explain first that procurement signed off on the schedule last month, then ask how the warehouse can make it work.
questions.x: Restating the specific facts and concern, then inviting correction, lets the other person confirm the picture before anyone argues for a solution. Leading with the sign-off defends the plan before you have shown you understood the problem.

questions.t: In Weger's experiments, a paraphrase on its own did not make speakers feel more understood, but paraphrasing combined with follow-up questions did.
questions.f: In Weger's experiments, a paraphrase on its own made speakers feel more understood, but adding follow-up questions to the paraphrase gave no further benefit.
questions.x: The 2010 study found a bare paraphrase mainly made the listener seem more likable; the 2014 follow-up, which paired paraphrasing with requests for more detail, raised feeling understood. So follow a restatement with a genuine question.

questions.t: To coach a junior analyst's status memo with a quick-screen edit, highlight the bottom-line sentence, mark passive verbs and jargon, and hand it back asking them to move the highlight to the top and fix only what is marked.
questions.f: To coach a junior analyst's status memo with a quick-screen edit, rewrite the whole memo yourself in clean style and hand it back as the model to copy next time.
questions.x: The quick-screen edit is one fast read that marks problems and leaves the fixing to the writer, so the analyst learns the pattern. A full rewrite is slower and teaches less.

questions.t: The 1986 Army pamphlet Effective Writing for Army Leaders told leaders to insist on the bottom line first, crediting the habit to business writers.
questions.f: The 1986 Army pamphlet Effective Writing for Army Leaders told leaders to insist on the bottom line first, presenting the habit as a new Army invention.
questions.x: DA Pam 600-67 is the earliest official BLUF instruction found, but it explicitly says business writers already did this. Later Army texts gave the habit the BLUF name.

questions.t: The Army pamphlet's clarity index adds average sentence length to the percentage of words of three or more syllables, with a target of about 30.
questions.f: The Army pamphlet's clarity index adds average sentence length to the percentage of words of three or more syllables, with a target of below 20.
questions.x: About 30 was the aim; scores under 20 were called abrupt and over 40 hard to read. It is a rule of thumb that counts length, not whether readers understand.

questions.t: Before sending a decision email, reread only the subject line and first two sentences and ask whether a busy reader could act correctly on those alone.
questions.f: Before sending a decision email, reread it top to bottom and check that the background builds logically toward the request in the closing paragraph.
questions.x: The BLUF self-check tests the opening, because many readers stop there. A message that builds to the ask at the end is the buried structure BLUF is meant to fix.

questions.t: When writing serious bad news to a reader likely to react with anger, you can explain the reasons before the news, but you must still state the news clearly rather than hide it.
questions.f: When writing serious bad news to a reader likely to react with anger, open with the decision in the first line anyway, because bottom line up front suits every work message.
questions.x: Textbooks keep the direct order for routine news and readers who want it, and allow an explain-first order when bluntness could cause anger. BLUF is a choice made by audience analysis, not a universal rule.

questions.t: Leading with the bottom line fits how people read: in Kieras's 1979 experiments, readers usually built a passage's main idea from its opening sentences.
questions.f: Leading with the bottom line fits how people read: in Kieras's 1979 experiments, readers usually built a passage's main idea from its closing sentences.
questions.x: A theme sentence placed first shaped readers' summaries more than the same sentence mid-passage. BLUF itself remains practitioner advice, since no controlled study has compared message orders directly.

questions.t: After a missed release, a manager tells the team, "My read is the handoff broke down somewhere. What would help us hit the next date?" In Gibb's terms she is using provisionalism and problem orientation, cues that lower defensiveness.
questions.f: After a missed release, a manager tells the team, "My read is the handoff broke down somewhere. What would help us hit the next date?" In Gibb's terms she is using strategy and neutrality, cues that raise defensiveness.
questions.x: "My read is" offers a view open to correction (provisionalism) and the question frames a shared problem rather than dictating a fix. Strategy means a hidden agenda and neutrality means detachment; neither shows here.

questions.t: To raise a late delivery without putting the analyst on guard, say "The build shipped four days after the date in the plan" rather than "Your estimates were way off again."
questions.f: To raise a late delivery without putting the analyst on guard, say "Your estimates were way off again" rather than "The build shipped four days after the date in the plan," so the cause is named up front.
questions.x: Describing an observable fact invites problem-solving, while a verdict on the person triggers a defence of the method. In the article's example, that defence crowded out the real cause, a late scope change.

questions.t: A 2015 meta-analysis of self-affirmation tests found a small effect on accepting threatening messages (d = 0.17) and a larger one on behaviour (d = 0.32).
questions.f: A 2015 meta-analysis of self-affirmation tests found a larger effect on accepting threatening messages (d = 0.32) and a small one on behaviour (d = 0.17).
questions.x: The effect on behaviour was the larger of the two; acceptance moved only slightly. Most of these studies used health messages, so the workplace payoff is plausible rather than proven.

questions.t: Asked if the new date is realistic, an engineer who privately thinks it is impossible tells her manager, "Sure, we'll make it work," as she always does with bosses. That is the over-compliant reflex that distorts a boss relationship.
questions.f: Asked if the new date is realistic, an engineer who privately thinks it is impossible tells her manager, "Sure, we'll make it work," as she always does with bosses. That is managing up done well, adapting to the boss.
questions.x: Swallowing disagreement is one of the authority reflexes Gabarro and Kotter warn about. Managing up rests on dependable candour, so she should flag the risk now, ideally with a proposed fix.

questions.t: If your manager keeps rewriting your weekly update at the last minute, ask in your one-on-one how they use it, then send it in the form and at the time that use requires.
questions.f: If your manager keeps rewriting your weekly update at the last minute, make the narrative email longer and more polished so there is less left for them to change.
questions.x: In the article's example the manager forwarded the update to a director and needed only decisions, risks and progress, a day earlier. Checking how the boss actually uses information beats guessing harder.

questions.t: Harvard professors John Gabarro and John Kotter set out the idea of managing up in their 1980 Harvard Business Review article "Managing Your Boss."
questions.f: Harvard professors John Gabarro and John Kotter set out the idea of managing up in their 1993 Academy of Management Review article "Managing Your Boss."
questions.x: "Managing Your Boss" appeared in HBR in 1980 and was reprinted as a classic in 2005. The 1993 Academy of Management Review paper was Dutton and Ashford's work on issue selling.

questions.t: After a client workshop, a lead tells the presenter, "You're a natural presenter!" In Hattie and Timperley's terms that is self-level feedback, the kind that carries the least usable information.
questions.f: After a client workshop, a lead tells the presenter, "You're a natural presenter!" In Hattie and Timperley's terms that is process-level feedback, the kind with the most powerful effect.
questions.x: It praises the person, not the work, so there is nothing to repeat. Process feedback would name what worked, such as opening with the client's own churn numbers before the recommendations.

questions.t: When asking a colleague for input on your work, say which kind you need (appreciation, coaching or evaluation) and ask a narrow question such as "What's one thing I could do differently?"
questions.f: When asking a colleague for input on your work, ask a broad "Any feedback for me?" and leave it to them to decide which kind of feedback to give.
questions.x: Heen notes people want different kinds of feedback at different times, and evaluation can drown out the coaching inside it. Naming the kind and narrowing the question makes the answer usable.

questions.t: Feedback intervention theory holds that feedback helps most when it keeps attention on the task and how to learn it, and loses power as it pulls attention toward the person's self-image.
questions.f: Feedback intervention theory holds that feedback helps most when it draws attention to the person's standing and self-image, and loses power as it stays narrowly on the task.
questions.x: Kluger and DeNisi explained feedback's mixed results by where it sends attention. Comments about the self pull focus away from the work, which is why the same conversation can lift or sink performance.

questions.t: Before a pricing call, a sales lead plans to build rapport by copying the client's posture and gestures. That treats a sign of being in sync as a lever, which the original account of rapport does not support.
questions.f: Before a pricing call, a sales lead plans to build rapport by copying the client's posture and gestures. That is the core rapport-building move the research recommends most often.
questions.x: Mirroring emerges once people are coordinated; it is not a technique to perform. The research most often builds rapport through active listening, personal interest and self-disclosure, with body cues in only about a tenth of studies.

questions.t: If a tense negotiation with a new counterpart will run mostly by email, have a short live call first, with a little non-business talk, before the written exchange starts.
questions.f: If a tense negotiation with a new counterpart will run mostly by email, keep everything in writing from the first message so the record stays clean and nothing personal gets in the way.
questions.x: Email strips out the cues that build rapport, and a brief non-business call before an email negotiation led to better economic and social outcomes. A purely written start is where impasses were most common.

questions.t: In Tickle-Degnen and Rosenthal's model, positivity and attentiveness carry the most weight in a first meeting, while coordination matters more as the relationship lengthens.
questions.f: In Tickle-Degnen and Rosenthal's model, coordination carries the most weight in a first meeting, while positivity and attentiveness matter more as the relationship lengthens.
questions.x: Early on, people are sizing each other up and following politeness norms, so warmth and focus dominate. Being smoothly in sync is the part that grows in importance over a longer relationship.

questions.t: During the round robin of a nominal group session, a junior analyst reads out her idea and a senior lead cuts in, "We tried that, it won't work." That is debate leaking into the round robin, which the facilitator should stop.
questions.f: During the round robin of a nominal group session, a junior analyst reads out her idea and a senior lead cuts in, "We tried that, it won't work." That is the clarification stage working as intended.
questions.x: The round robin only records ideas, with no evaluation; even clarification is limited to explaining items, not judging them. Early critique from a senior voice brings back the blocking and status effects NGT exists to remove.

questions.t: Once the numbered list of ideas has been clarified, have each person privately rank their top five items and tally the scores in front of the group before discussing priorities.
questions.f: Once the numbered list of ideas has been clarified, open a group discussion of which items matter most and finish with a show of hands on the favourites.
questions.x: Private ranking lets everyone weigh in before seniors' preferences are visible. An open debate and a public vote let the first strong voice anchor the room, the problem the method is built to avoid.

questions.t: Diehl and Stroebe traced most of the idea shortfall in interacting brainstorming groups to production blocking: only one person can speak at a time, so others forget or hold back ideas while waiting.
questions.f: Diehl and Stroebe traced most of the idea shortfall in interacting brainstorming groups to social loafing: members coast on others' effort because their own contribution can't be identified.
questions.x: Their experiments pinned the loss on waiting for a turn to talk, which is why NGT starts with silent, individual writing. Loafing is a different explanation from the one their work identified.

questions.t: A candidate with no data on a role's pay band asks the hiring manager what range the company had in mind before naming any number. Holding back fits first-offer guidance, because the other side knows the range better.
questions.f: A candidate with no data on a role's pay band asks the hiring manager what range the company had in mind before naming any number. That throws away the first-mover advantage, since opening first always pays.
questions.x: The advantage depends on information: move first when you know the zone of agreement at least as well as the other side. Uninformed openers in Maaravi and Levy's studies landed far off the market in both directions.

questions.t: Having found that similar analytics retainers cost $8K-11K a month, a buyer should open with a precise figure near the low end, give a one-sentence reason, then stop and listen.
questions.f: Having found that similar analytics retainers cost $8K-11K a month, a buyer should say there is no fixed budget yet and ask what the agency would normally charge.
questions.x: Knowing the market as well as the agency, she can set the reference point herself with a stated rationale. Asking them to name a price invites an anchor at the top of the range.

questions.t: A 2025 meta-analysis of 90 negotiation studies found the size of the first offer correlated strongly with the final agreement value (r = .62).
questions.f: A 2025 meta-analysis of 90 negotiation studies found the size of the first offer correlated only weakly with the final agreement value (r = .16).
questions.x: The pull of the opening number on the final deal was strong, which is why the effect is rated robust. The same analysis also found that very ambitious openings led to more impasses.

questions.t: At a trade-show demo, a visiting client keeps stepping closer as a sales engineer talks, and the engineer silently labels him pushy. That reads a likely difference in distance norms as a flaw of character.
questions.f: At a trade-show demo, a visiting client keeps stepping closer as a sales engineer talks, and the engineer silently labels him pushy. That is an accurate read, since closing distance reliably signals pushiness.
questions.x: People tend to blame closeness on the person rather than on a cultural norm. The better move is to assume a norm difference first and adjust, since comfortable distances vary by culture, gender and age.

questions.t: When meeting a new client in person, start at a neutral social distance, watch whether they step back or lean in, and adjust your distance to them.
questions.f: When meeting a new client in person, keep to the distance that feels comfortable to you throughout, so that you come across as steady and consistent.
questions.x: Distance norms differ between people and cultures, so the fix is to match and adapt. Holding your own comfort zone can make you seem aloof to a close-contact person or intrusive to a distant one.

questions.t: In a 2017 study of nearly 9,000 people in 42 countries, the average comfortable talking distance was about 135 cm for a stranger and about 92 cm for an acquaintance.
questions.f: In a 2017 study of nearly 9,000 people in 42 countries, the average comfortable talking distance was about 92 cm for a stranger and about 135 cm for an acquaintance.
questions.x: People wanted strangers farther away than acquaintances, with close others nearest at about 32 cm. Countries differed considerably, and the study measured stated preferences rather than behaviour.

questions.t: A support lead opens her ops-review proposal by tying a billing-page fix to leadership's customer-retention goal for the year. In Dutton and colleagues' terms, that is a packaging move.
questions.f: A support lead opens her ops-review proposal by tying a billing-page fix to leadership's customer-retention goal for the year. In Dutton and colleagues' terms, that is a process move.
questions.x: Packaging means presenting the issue as a business case bundled with goals leaders already own. Process moves concern homework, channels and timing, such as choosing the scheduled ops review as the forum.

questions.t: When raising a long-ignored problem with leadership, bring the data, a scoped fix and the one decision you want, rather than writing that nobody seems to care.
questions.f: When raising a long-ignored problem with leadership, make your frustration plain, since showing how strongly the team feels is what gets an issue onto the agenda.
questions.x: Pitching from frustration is the most common mistake; passion can tip into anger on both sides. A calm business case with a proposed solution and a specific ask gives leaders something to decide.

questions.t: The main evidence for issue-selling moves comes from retrospective accounts by managers at a single hospital, so the moves are linked to success but have not been tested in controlled trials.
questions.f: The main evidence for issue-selling moves comes from large controlled trials across many companies, so the moves are known to cause leaders to act on raised issues.
questions.x: The 2001 study gathered 82 recalled accounts from one nonprofit hospital, and its authors note it mostly confirms standard change advice. That is why the technique is rated mixed rather than robust.

questions.t: A data scientist who knows her model best keeps asking her lead to present it to executives, saying "presenting isn't really my thing." That handing-off is a common way speaking anxiety works against a career.
questions.f: A data scientist who knows her model best keeps asking her lead to present it to executives, saying "presenting isn't really my thing." That is sensible delegation that keeps her work visible.
questions.x: Speaking anxiety often operates through avoidance: others brief the executives, so the person's work is seen less than it should be. The self-check is whether she is declining because it isn't her job or because she fears it.

questions.t: To build tolerance for speaking, volunteer for short, low-stakes slots such as a two-minute stand-up update before taking on a long, high-stakes briefing.
questions.f: To build tolerance for speaking, take on the longest, highest-stakes briefing you can get first, so that every smaller talk afterwards feels easy.
questions.x: The evidence comes mostly from cognitive and behavioural programmes that use graded exposure. Repeated small steps closer to the real setting build tolerance; jumping straight to the hardest case is not what those programmes do.

questions.t: A 2019 meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials found psychological treatments reduced fear of public speaking with a moderate-to-large effect (g = 0.74) that grew larger at follow-up.
questions.f: A 2019 meta-analysis of 30 randomized trials found psychological treatments reduced fear of public speaking with a moderate-to-large effect (g = 0.74) that had faded by follow-up.
questions.x: The effect rose to g = 1.11 at follow-up, suggesting people kept improving after treatment. Self-reported gains were larger than physiological or behavioural ones, and small trial arms are a limit.

questions.t: A director asks her team, "What should we do about the vendor?", listens to twenty minutes of ideas, then announces the plan she had drafted beforehand, unchanged. That is asking then ignoring, which teaches people the door isn't really open.
questions.f: A director asks her team, "What should we do about the vendor?", listens to twenty minutes of ideas, then announces the plan she had drafted beforehand, unchanged. That is humble inquiry, since she asked before deciding.
questions.x: Humble inquiry needs real curiosity and a willingness to learn something that changes your view. Asking for input and deciding exactly as planned shows the question was a formality.

questions.t: When a report hands in a client analysis in an unexpected format the day before the review, ask them to walk you through what they were going for before asking for any changes.
questions.f: When a report hands in a client analysis in an unexpected format the day before the review, tell them to redo it in the standard template tonight and discuss their reasoning after the review.
questions.x: Asking first surfaces reasons the lead may not know, such as a client request, and still leaves time to agree a format. Telling first assumes the lead already has all the information and shuts the report down.

questions.t: In Huang and colleagues' experiments, asking more questions made people better liked largely because their partners said more about themselves in response.
questions.f: In Huang and colleagues' experiments, asking more questions made people better liked largely because the askers came across as more competent and better informed.
questions.x: Extra disclosure by the partner accounted for much of the rise in liking. The effects were small to moderate and come from a nearby behaviour, since humble inquiry itself is untested practitioner advice.

questions.topic: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
questions.t: In Daft and Lengel's theory, equivocality means competing interpretations of a situation, reduced only by exchanging views, while uncertainty means missing data, reduced by more information.
questions.f: In Daft and Lengel's theory, uncertainty means competing interpretations of a situation, reduced only by exchanging views, while equivocality means missing data, reduced by more information.
questions.x: The distinction drives channel choice: a lean report can fill a data gap, but differing readings of a situation need a rich, two-way channel. A schedule update is uncertainty; a disputed reorganisation is equivocality.

questions.topic: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
questions.t: A director walks over to tell a long-serving engineer about a reorganisation in person, partly to show that she cares. Daft and colleagues' companion study would class that as a symbolic reason for the channel choice.
questions.f: A director walks over to tell a long-serving engineer about a reorganisation in person, partly to show that she cares. Daft and colleagues' companion study would class that as a situational reason for the channel choice.
questions.x: Symbolic reasons concern what the medium itself signals, such as importance or care. Situational reasons are practical limits like time and distance, which are not what drove this choice.

questions.topic: Message Equivocality, Media Selection, and Manager Performance
questions.t: In Lengel and Daft's 1984 study of 95 managers, the share choosing face-to-face rose from about 14% to 84% as an incident's interpretive load increased.
questions.f: In Lengel and Daft's 1984 study of 95 managers, the share choosing face-to-face fell from about 84% to 14% as an incident's interpretive load increased.
questions.x: More ambiguous incidents pushed managers toward richer channels, while addressed written documents fell from about 62% to 11%. These were self-reported choices at one petrochemical company.

questions.t: A database engineer writes a design note for fellow database specialists and keeps the technical terms they all use. That can still be plain language, because the right level depends on who is reading.
questions.f: A database engineer writes a design note for fellow database specialists and keeps the technical terms they all use. That breaks plain language, which means avoiding technical terms whatever the audience.
questions.x: Plain language is defined by whether the intended readers can find, understand and use the text; treating it as dumbing down is a common myth. Specialists' shared terms help them, though the same note for clients would need everyday words.

questions.t: In a client update, replace "P1 defects have been remediated; cutover is contingent on CAB sign-off" with "We fixed the urgent bugs your team found, and we can switch over once our change board approves it, likely Thursday."
questions.f: In a client update, keep "P1 defects have been remediated; cutover is contingent on CAB sign-off" and add a glossary at the end defining P1, cutover and CAB.
questions.x: The rewrite names who acts, swaps internal acronyms for the reader's words and says what happens next. A glossary at the end makes the reader hunt; terms that must stay should be defined where they first appear.

questions.t: A 2022 systematic review of plain language summaries of research concluded that most criteria in plain-language writing guidelines did not yet have empirical support.
questions.f: A 2022 systematic review of plain language summaries of research concluded that most criteria in plain-language writing guidelines were backed by consistent experimental evidence.
questions.x: Whole rewrites for an audience tend to help, but studies rarely isolate which rule did the work, so individual guidelines remain unproven. That gap is why plain language is rated mixed rather than robust.

questions.t: The most junior person in a cross-team review tells herself, "Priya, you spotted a real gap. Ask one short question about the churn assumption, then let the lead answer." That is distanced self-talk.
questions.f: The most junior person in a cross-team review tells herself, "Priya, you spotted a real gap. Ask one short question about the churn assumption, then let the lead answer." That is anxiety reappraisal.
questions.x: The tell is coaching herself by name, as "you", which shifts her vantage point rather than relabelling her racing heart as excitement. Reappraisal changes what the arousal means; distancing changes who is looking.

questions.t: Use distanced self-talk to steady yourself before a tense meeting, but switch back to "I" when you make a personal commitment, such as "I will raise the risk at Thursday's review."
questions.f: Use distanced self-talk to steady yourself before a tense meeting, and keep using your own name even when you make a personal commitment, such as "Sam will raise the risk at Thursday's review."
questions.x: Seeing yourself from outside may weaken identification with your future self, so researchers suggest the first person for commitments. Distancing is for appraising the moment, not for owning the promise.

questions.t: In 2016 spotlight-effect experiments, people imagining an embarrassing entrance in the first person guessed about 47-48% of the room would notice, versus about 27-30% with a third-person view.
questions.f: In 2016 spotlight-effect experiments, people imagining an embarrassing entrance in the first person guessed about 27-30% of the room would notice, versus about 47-48% with a third-person view.
questions.x: The observer's vantage point brought estimates closer to the real noticing rate and cut embarrassment. The samples were small and from one university, so treat it as suggestive.

questions.t: A project lead tells a peer who skipped the design review, "I think we see the review differently. I'd like to hear how you see it, then explain why it matters to me before release." That opens from the third story.
questions.f: A project lead tells a peer who skipped the design review, "I think we see the review differently. I'd like to hear how you see it, then explain why it matters to me before release." That opens by arguing the facts first.
questions.x: The lead describes the gap between their views as a neutral observer would and invites the peer to explore it, rather than leading with "You keep ignoring the review process." Listening first, then speaking for yourself, follows the worksheet's order.

questions.t: When a colleague's remark in a meeting stung, keep their intent separate from its impact on you, rather than assuming they meant the harm you felt.
questions.f: When a colleague's remark in a meeting stung, treat the impact on you as evidence of what they meant, and say so plainly so the issue is named.
questions.x: People tend to judge others by impact and themselves by intent, which keeps the "what happened" conversation stuck in blame. Describe the impact on you and ask what they intended.

questions.t: In Levine and Cohen's 2018 studies, people expected honest conversations to go worse than they did, mainly because they overestimated how negatively the other person would react.
questions.f: In Levine and Cohen's 2018 studies, people expected honest conversations to go better than they did, mainly because they underestimated how negatively the other person would react.
questions.x: Those who actually had the conversations found them more enjoyable and connecting than forecasters predicted. The samples were mostly students or online, so it shows a general bias, not a promise about a given talk.

questions.t: A project manager asks a peer for two ideas to keep kick-offs on time. The peer suggests sending the agenda a day early, and he replies, "We tried that; clients don't read it." That breaks feedforward's no-debate rule.
questions.f: A project manager asks a peer for two ideas to keep kick-offs on time. The peer suggests sending the agenda a day early, and he replies, "We tried that; clients don't read it." That is feedforward done well, testing each idea as it arrives.
questions.x: In feedforward the only reply is "thank you"; you write the idea down and decide later whether to try it. Rebutting on the spot turns the exchange back into a debate and discourages further suggestions.

questions.t: Rather than asking for feedback on last week's overrun kick-off, say "I'm working on running kick-offs that finish on time. Could you give me two ideas to try at the next one?"
questions.f: Rather than asking for ideas for the next kick-off, ask "Could you give me feedback on last week's kick-off? It ran over, but the client kept raising scope questions."
questions.x: The forward version names a goal, bounds the request to two ideas and avoids reopening the past. Asking about last week while explaining the overrun opens with a defence, so the colleague has to argue to be useful.

questions.t: The Feedforward Interview, an appraisal conversation that starts from an employee's recent success and what made it possible, was proposed by Kluger and Nir in 2010.
questions.f: The Feedforward Interview, an appraisal conversation that starts from an employee's recent success and what made it possible, was proposed by Marshall Goldsmith in 2010.
questions.x: Two methods share the name. Goldsmith's is a quick peer exchange of suggestions from his workshops; Kluger and Nir's is a structured manager-employee interview built on appreciative inquiry.

questions.t: A teammate says she's worried her client demo will flop, and her lead replies at once, "Don't worry, you'll be great!" Rogers and Farson would count that quick reassurance as a response that can shut down honest talk.
questions.f: A teammate says she's worried her client demo will flop, and her lead replies at once, "Don't worry, you'll be great!" Rogers and Farson would count that as active listening, since it answers the feeling behind her words.
questions.x: Reassurance skips understanding: it tells her how to feel instead of showing he grasped what worries her. Reflecting the worry and asking what concerns her most would keep her talking.

questions.t: In a heated disagreement over priorities, restate the other person's point to their satisfaction before you state your own view.
questions.f: In a heated disagreement over priorities, state your own view briefly first so they know where you stand, then restate their point.
questions.x: Rogers and Farson proposed this discipline because being understood lowers the threat that makes people defend their position. Leading with your view invites a counter-argument before they feel heard.

questions.t: In a 2024 meta-analysis of feeling listened to at work, the link with job performance fell to about r = .21 when only other-rated data were used.
questions.f: In a 2024 meta-analysis of feeling listened to at work, the link with job performance rose to about r = .61 when only other-rated data were used.
questions.x: About three-quarters of the pooled data were self-reports, which inflate associations. Removing that bias shrank the performance link, though it remained positive.

questions.t: A supplier sends a client three contract packages, but one is clearly better for the supplier and the other two are padded to look worse. That is not a MESO, because each package should be worth about the same to the offerer.
questions.f: A supplier sends a client three contract packages, but one is clearly better for the supplier and the other two are padded to look worse. That is a MESO done well, steering the client toward the preferred option.
questions.x: Hiding a favourite among decoys defeats the point: you should be content with whichever option they pick, and claiming you would accept any of them must be true. Decoys cross from strategy into deception.

questions.t: When a client answers your three packages by combining the best term from each, reply with a fresh set of equivalent packages built from your scoring, rather than conceding term by term.
questions.f: When a client answers your three packages by combining the best term from each, accept the combination if it is close to your target, to keep goodwill and close quickly.
questions.x: Cherry-picking takes each package's best concession and leaves you worse off than any of the options you offered. New equivalent packages keep the trade-offs intact and still use what their choice revealed.

questions.t: In Leonardelli and colleagues' experiments, MESOs anchored counteroffers more strongly than single offers because recipients saw them as a more sincere effort to reach agreement.
questions.f: In Leonardelli and colleagues' experiments, MESOs anchored counteroffers more strongly than single offers because recipients felt overloaded by the options and settled for the first one.
questions.x: Perceived sincerity made the offers stronger reference points, especially when they were ambitious. Choice overload is a reason to cap MESOs at two or three packages, not the source of their pull.

questions.t: Mapping an expense-tool rollout, an ops manager notes the payroll lead must sign off the export file but has little interest in the project. On the power-interest grid, that stakeholder should be kept satisfied.
questions.f: Mapping an expense-tool rollout, an ops manager notes the payroll lead must sign off the export file but has little interest in the project. On the power-interest grid, that stakeholder needs only to be kept informed.
questions.x: Sign-off is power, so this is the high-power, lower-interest quadrant: a targeted briefing and timely sign-off, not just the go-live email. Keep informed is for those low on both power and interest.

questions.t: Before replacing a tool your whole department uses, give each stakeholder group its own message, messenger, channel and timing based on its power and concerns, rather than one all-staff announcement.
questions.f: Before replacing a tool your whole department uses, send one clear all-staff announcement two weeks before go-live, so that everyone gets the same message at the same time.
questions.x: A single email treats everyone as one audience and surprises the people who could block the launch or will feel it most. Not everyone needs everything, but everyone needs something.

questions.t: Stakeholder salience theory holds that the stakeholders who get most attention are those seen to hold power, legitimacy and urgency at the same time.
questions.f: Stakeholder salience theory holds that the stakeholders who get most attention are those seen to hold power, interest and influence at the same time.
questions.x: Mitchell, Agle and Wood's three attributes are power, legitimacy and urgency, and all three are perceptions that shift over time. Power and interest are the axes of the separate grid.

questions.t: Working through D.A.E. after a tense call, a manager writes as step one: "She was rude to the client." That line is already an evaluation smuggled into the description.
questions.f: Working through D.A.E. after a tense call, a manager writes as step one: "She was rude to the client." That line is a sound description, since it reports what happened on the call.
questions.x: "Rude" is a judgement measured against the manager's own norms. A description is what a camera would catch, such as "she ended the call without summarising next steps," which people who disagree could still accept.

questions.t: If a newly transferred engineer stays silent in design reviews and emails good concerns afterwards, name that pattern and ask how disagreements were raised on teams they've worked on.
questions.f: If a newly transferred engineer stays silent in design reviews and emails good concerns afterwards, tell them to say it in the room, since emailing later looks like going around the team.
questions.x: The better reply leads with the observable pattern, allows several explanations and checks before judging. The worse one presents an evaluation, going around the team, as fact, when the engineer may follow a different norm.

questions.t: In 2008 Kyoung-Ah Nam and John Condon proposed renaming the D.I.E. exercise D.A.E., partly because "interpret" and "evaluate" are near-synonyms in everyday speech.
questions.f: In 2008 Janet and Milton Bennett proposed renaming the D.I.E. exercise D.A.E., partly because "interpret" and "evaluate" are near-synonyms in everyday speech.
questions.x: The Bennetts adapted the exercise for intercultural workshops in 1975; the D.A.E. renaming came from Nam and Condon decades later. They also noted trainers kept apologising for the D.I.E. acronym.

questions.t: A team charter says cameras are optional at stand-up, but the lead keeps her own camera on every call and remarks whenever a tile goes dark. Her behaviour sets an unspoken cameras-on rule despite the written norm.
questions.f: A team charter says cameras are optional at stand-up, but the lead keeps her own camera on every call and remarks whenever a tile goes dark. The team has a working camera-optional norm, since it is written down.
questions.x: People read the real rule from what leaders do and reward, and the share of visible webcams strongly predicts whether others switch theirs on. The fix is to model it: switch off yourself and stop commenting on dark tiles.

questions.t: When setting a camera-optional norm, tell newer colleagues directly, one-to-one, that turning the camera off will not count against them.
questions.f: When setting a camera-optional norm, let newer colleagues pick it up by watching what the rest of the team does, so it doesn't feel like special treatment.
questions.x: In Shockley's experiment the fatigue cost of cameras-on was larger for newer employees, who feel most pressure to look attentive. Saying it to them directly removes the guesswork that watching others leaves.

questions.t: Bennett and colleagues' hourly surveys of employees found no significant link between camera use and post-meeting fatigue, while group belonging was the strongest buffer.
questions.f: Bennett and colleagues' hourly surveys of employees found camera use was the strongest predictor of post-meeting fatigue, while group belonging made no difference.
questions.x: Their study challenges the camera effect that Shockley's experiment found, which is why the evidence is mixed. Both point toward giving choice while keeping connection, for example with a short cameras-on check-in.

questions.t: Asked how many customers a price rise will cost, a product lead tells the leadership team, "Churn should be fine, though obviously nobody can be sure." That pairs false reassurance with a blanket hedge, leaving nothing to plan with.
questions.f: Asked how many customers a price rise will cost, a product lead tells the leadership team, "Churn should be fine, though obviously nobody can be sure." That is well-communicated uncertainty, since it admits nobody can be sure.
questions.x: Leaders can neither plan for the downside nor challenge the estimate. A better answer gives a best estimate, a plausible range, how solid the evidence is and when it will improve.

questions.t: When an executive asks something you can't answer yet, say "We don't know yet; here's what we're doing to find out, and we'll update you by Thursday."
questions.f: When an executive asks something you can't answer yet, give your best guess in a confident tone, so that you don't look unprepared in front of them.
questions.x: Crisis-communication guidance asks speakers to name what is unknown, what is being done and when they'll update. Projecting false certainty risks a decision built on a guess and costs credibility later.

questions.t: Gustafson and Rice's 2020 review found that technical uncertainty, such as ranges and probabilities, had only positive or null effects, while highlighting expert disagreement produced most of the negative effects.
questions.f: Gustafson and Rice's 2020 review found that highlighting expert disagreement had only positive or null effects, while technical uncertainty, such as ranges and probabilities, produced most of the negative effects.
questions.x: Ranges rarely backfired, so stating them is low-risk; it is consensus uncertainty that tends to cost belief and trust. The review pooled no effect sizes and mostly studied public audiences, not managers.

questions.t: Asked if the vendor migration is on track, a lead replies, "Most of the cutover tasks are done," though all of them are. Via the Quantity maxim, the manager will infer that some tasks are late.
questions.f: Asked if the vendor migration is on track, a lead replies, "Most of the cutover tasks are done," though all of them are. Via the Quality maxim, the manager will infer that some tasks are late.
questions.x: Listeners assume you are as informative as needed, so a weaker word like "most" implies the stronger "all" isn't true. Quality is about saying only what you believe and can back up, which the lead did.

questions.t: When a manager asks whether a project is on track, answer that question first and add background after, since opening with background suggests you're avoiding the answer.
questions.f: When a manager asks whether a project is on track, give the background first so the answer makes sense, and save the yes or no for the end of your reply.
questions.x: Listeners assume each contribution is relevant to the question, so a reply that starts elsewhere gets read as evasion. Answer, then add the context the reader needs.

questions.t: Grice's cooperative principle does not require being polite or agreeable: a curt, even evasive reply can still be cooperative in his minimal, rational sense.
questions.f: Grice's cooperative principle requires being polite and agreeable, so a curt or evasive reply breaks it and stops listeners inferring meaning.
questions.x: Reading cooperation as niceness is the misreading Davies calls cooperation drift. Grice described the expectations listeners use to work out meaning, which is why even a terse reply carries implications.

questions.t: A team lead's invite for a 45-minute meeting reads: "Agenda: 1. Office move update 2. Desk allocation 3. AOB." Those topic labels give the group no finish line for any item.
questions.f: A team lead's invite for a 45-minute meeting reads: "Agenda: 1. Office move update 2. Desk allocation 3. AOB." That is a well-designed agenda, since every item names an area to cover.
questions.x: A bare noun doesn't say what counts as done or whether people are deciding or listening. "(Decide, 15 min) Which two weeks in March should we move?" gives a question, a purpose and a time box.

questions.t: If you sit down to write a meeting's agenda and cannot phrase a single question the group needs to answer together, cancel the meeting.
questions.f: If you sit down to write a meeting's agenda and cannot phrase a single question the group needs to answer together, hold it anyway as an open check-in and let topics emerge.
questions.x: Rogelberg argues the questions should set who attends and when the meeting ends; no questions suggests there's nothing this group needs to settle. An open check-in is how unnecessary meetings survive.

questions.t: In Leach and colleagues' 2009 surveys, circulating a written agenda before the meeting was linked to higher perceived effectiveness, while one handed out only at the meeting showed no significant link.
